title: A* Search
body:
[[Best-First Search]] with the one evaluation function that gets you both speed and a guarantee:

$$f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$$

**$g(n)$ is what the path to $n$ has actually cost. $h(n)$ is the [[Heuristic]] guess at what
remains. $f(n)$ is therefore the estimated cost of the best solution *through* $n$**, and
expanding the smallest $f$ first means always working on the most promising complete route rather
than the most promising next step.

That one addition is the whole difference from greedy best-first, and it is why $A^*$ is the
algorithm every route planner and every game pathfinder actually runs.

## Optimality

**$A^*$ returns an optimal path whenever $h$ is [[Heuristic|admissible]]** (never overestimates
the true remaining cost).

The argument is short. Suppose a suboptimal goal $G_2$ is popped from the frontier. Somewhere on
the frontier there is a node $n$ on the optimal path to the real goal $G$. Then:

$$f(n) = g(n) + h(n) \le g(n) + h^*(n) = \text{cost}(G) < \text{cost}(G_2) = f(G_2)$$

using $h \le h^*$ for the first step and $h(G_2) = 0$ for the last. So $f(n) < f(G_2)$ and $n$
would have been popped first. Contradiction, so $G_2$ never gets popped before $G$.

**Consistency buys the stronger property.** If $h$ is consistent (the triangle inequality
$h(n) \le c(n, n') + h(n')$), then $f$ never decreases along a path and every node is expanded at
most once, so no node needs revisiting. Admissible-but-inconsistent heuristics still give optimal
answers but may require re-expanding nodes.

## The two corners it sits between

| | $f$ | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| $h = 0$ | $g$ | Dijkstra's algorithm. Optimal, and expands everything within the goal's cost radius |
| $h = h^*$ (perfect) | $g + h^*$ | walks straight down the optimal path, expanding nothing else |
| in between | $g + h$ | $A^*$. The better $h$, the fewer nodes expanded |

**So $A^*$ is Dijkstra plus a sense of direction**, and the whole art is in $h$. This is why
[[Heuristic]] is the note that matters most of the three: the algorithm is fixed, the heuristic is
the design work. [[Dijkstra's Algorithm]] has the implementation, in `Leetcode/`; the framing
here is the one that matters, and [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] carries the graph context.

## The cost nobody mentions

$A^*$ is optimal in nodes expanded for a given heuristic, and it still keeps **every** generated
node in memory. On a large map that is the binding constraint, not time, and it is why the
variants exist (IDA\*, memory-bounded $A^*$, and in games, hierarchical maps that shrink the graph
before searching it).
